prompt: /proto-research handbook-answers: our 3-person HR team gets about 20 questions a day in Slack that the employee handbook already answers (leave, expenses, notice periods). The handbook is one markdown file, 38 pages, about 40 KB, and it changes twice a year. We want a bot in the HR channel that answers from the handbook and says which section it used. A wrong answer costs a follow-up with HR, and HR reads the channel anyway. It's a new project, nothing exists yet. What retrieval design should we go with?
minimum_solution: One LLM call per question with the whole handbook (about 10,000 tokens, well inside a context window) placed in the prompt, instructed to answer only from it and to name the section, or to say the handbook does not cover it. A small Slack handler that passes the question in and posts the reply. The handbook is read from the file at call time, so the twice-yearly update is replacing the file. One document that fits in the prompt needs no retrieval step.

prompt: /proto-research runbook-search: our on-call engineers need to find the right runbook during incidents. There are about 6,000 markdown pages across our platform wiki, around 4 million tokens, and about 50 change on a normal day. Queries are a mix of exact error codes like E4021 and plain descriptions like 'payments queue backing up'. Around 200 searches a week. It should give a short answer with links to the pages it used. If it invents a step, someone could run it on production, so it has to say when it found nothing. New project. What should the retrieval pipeline look like?
minimum_solution: Chunk pages by heading. One store that holds both a keyword index and embeddings, because exact error codes need keyword match and plain descriptions need semantic match; merge the two rankings with a simple fusion such as reciprocal rank fusion. One LLM call that answers only from the retrieved chunks and links them. Return 'nothing found' with no generated answer when retrieval scores fall below a threshold. A nightly batch re-index of changed pages. A small set of real past queries with known correct pages to check retrieval and set the threshold.

prompt: /proto-research classifier-regression-check: I maintain a small service that calls Claude with one prompt to sort inbound support emails into 4 queues. I already have 150 emails hand-labelled with the right queue, in a CSV. I keep tweaking the prompt and I can't tell whether a change made things worse. A misroute costs a few minutes when an agent moves the email by hand. It's just me working on this and I change the prompt maybe once a month. What should I set up for evaluating prompt changes?
minimum_solution: A script run by hand that sends the 150 labelled emails through the prompt, computes overall accuracy and a per-queue confusion count against the CSV labels, saves the result to a file, and prints the difference from the previous saved result. The labels already exist and the output is one of 4 categories, so exact match is the whole grading step.

prompt: /proto-research summary-model-switch: we generate summaries of customer calls for account managers, who read them before renewal conversations. We want to decide whether to move to a cheaper model. We have about 2,000 stored transcripts and the current summaries, but no labels of any kind. The main worry is a summary stating something that wasn't said on the call, because an account manager could repeat it to the customer. Two PMs can give us a few hours of review time. This is a one-off decision we need to make next month, not an ongoing programme. How should we evaluate this?
minimum_solution: Sample about 50 transcripts. Generate summaries from both models. The two PMs label each summary pass or fail on one criterion: does it state anything not in the transcript. Check that the two PMs agree on an overlapping subset. Compare the two models on the same transcripts with a paired count of failures, reported with its uncertainty. A single-criterion LLM judge is optional, and only if calibrated against the PM labels to extend coverage. Run once, by a script, with the result written to a document.

prompt: /proto-research ci-failure-digest: I want an agent for our team that goes through last night's failed CI runs on our main repo each morning and posts a summary in our engineering Slack channel saying what failed and the likely reason from the logs. Usually 0 to 5 failures a night. We'd read it over coffee, and if it gets a reason wrong someone opens the log like they do today. It only ever reads CI and posts one message, it never touches code or re-runs anything. New project. What agent design should we use?
minimum_solution: A scheduled script with a fixed sequence and no loop: fetch last night's failed runs from the CI API, trim each log to its failing section, make one LLM call per failure or one for the batch, post one Slack message, and post nothing or a 'no failures' line when there were none. The steps are known in advance, so no tool-choosing loop, agent framework or memory is needed.

prompt: /proto-research refund-agent: we handle about 300 refund requests a week through our support inbox. We want an agent that reads a request, looks up the order, checks it against our refund policy, then either issues the refund or passes it to a person. We already have internal APIs for order lookup and for issuing a refund, and the policy is a 4-page document. Policy allows automatic refunds up to 50 EUR within 30 days of delivery; everything else needs a person. The path through a request varies: some are missing the order number, some cover several orders. A wrong refund costs real money and can't be pulled back easily. New project on top of those APIs. What should the agent loop look like?
minimum_solution: A single tool-use loop with a small set of tools: look up order, issue refund, and hand off to a person, with the policy text in the system prompt. An iteration cap that hands off to a person when reached. The 50 EUR and 30-day limits enforced in code inside the issue-refund tool, not left to the model, and an idempotency check so one request cannot refund twice. A log of every tool call and decision. A case with a missing order number or several orders can look up or hand off within the same loop, so one agent is enough.

prompt: /proto-research sms-copy-guardrails: our marketing tool uses an LLM to draft promotional SMS messages, about 400 a month, and a marketer reviews each one before sending. Legal has two hard rules: a message must be 160 characters or fewer, and it must end with the exact text 'Reply STOP to opt out'. Drafts break these rules often enough to annoy the marketers. If a message that breaks the rule goes out we have a compliance problem, though the marketer is there to catch it. New feature in an existing Python service. What guardrails should we put around the model?
minimum_solution: A deterministic validator in code that checks length is at most 160 characters and that the message ends with the exact opt-out text. On failure, one or two retries with the specific violation fed back to the model; if it still fails, show the marketer the failure rather than the draft as valid. Both rules can be computed, so no model or classifier is needed to check them.

prompt: /proto-research order-assistant-isolation: we're adding a logged-in chat assistant to our shop that answers questions about a customer's own orders, about 2,000 conversations a day. It calls one read-only tool, get_orders. Security's concern is that someone uses prompt injection to get the assistant to show another customer's orders, which would be a reportable data breach. Everything else it could say wrong is low stakes, because it can only read orders and a person can correct it. We launch in 3 weeks. What guardrails do we need?
minimum_solution: Take the customer id from the authenticated session in the tool layer, and do not expose it as a parameter the model can set, so get_orders can only return the logged-in customer's rows whatever the model is persuaded to do. An automated test that attempts to reach another customer's orders, including with an injected id, and shows it cannot. Logging of tool calls. The authorization boundary sits in code, so the breach is prevented without needing to detect injection.
